headline: A 2016 federal law that targets opioid abuse through prevention, treatment, law enforcement, veterans' care, and changes to prescribing and drug-monitoring rules.
what_it_does: The law sets up many federal programs to fight opioid misuse and addiction. It funds grants for naloxone access, treatment, recovery groups, and state prescription drug monitoring programs, and it asks agencies to study and report on pain management, neonatal abstinence syndrome, and related issues. It also changes certain rules, such as how the FDA reviews opioid drug applications, how pharmacists can partially fill certain prescriptions, and how the VA handles opioid therapy and provider oversight.

who_it_affects.how: The VA must expand opioid safety efforts, make naloxone more available, and add patient advocacy and complementary health programs, and high-risk veterans may skip copayments for overdose treatments and related education.
They may partially fill certain schedule II prescriptions, such as opioids, if state law allows and the patient or prescriber asks for it.
They can qualify to prescribe medications for opioid use disorder in office-based programs when working with or under a physician, if state law requires that oversight.
They may set up drug management programs for beneficiaries at risk of prescription drug abuse and must track certain usage patterns.

who_it_affects.group: State governments and state prescription drug monitoring programs
who_it_affects.how: States can receive grants to run and expand monitoring programs and must share aggregate data with HHS and help prescribers use the system.

who_it_affects.group: Pregnant and postpartum women with substance use disorders
who_it_affects.how: Residential and outpatient treatment programs they use can receive expanded federal support, including child care services for their children.

who_it_affects.group: Families of infants born affected by substance exposure
who_it_affects.how: States must develop plans of safe care that address the infant's and family's treatment needs as a condition of certain child protective services grants.

who_it_affects.group: Youth sports participants and their families
who_it_affects.how: HHS must study how information about opioid risks after sports injuries is shared and may help develop better information.
The GAO must study the collateral consequences they face, such as legal or administrative penalties after sentencing.

when_it_takes_effect: Most provisions took effect on enactment on July 22, 2016, but many grant programs, reports, and changes have their own start and end dates, and some run through fiscal year 2021.
